Wang Rong.lab_name: Pérez Lab, Linus Pauling Institute, Oregon State University (affiliation on WAN2017) (Corvallis, Oregon, USA)
Wang Rong.role: Researcher in Viviana Pérez's group at the Linus Pauling Institute who studied how rapamycin holds back cellular senescence, and first author of work separating its effect on the senescence secretory profile from its Nrf2-dependent effect on cell-cycle arrest
Wang Rong.sub: Linus Pauling Institute and Department of Biochemistry & Biophysics, Oregon State University (papers with Viviana Pérez, 2014–2022)
story: Rong Wang was first author of the Atlas study from Viviana Pérez's group at Oregon State University asking whether rapamycin needs the transcription factor Nrf2 to hold back cellular senescence (WAN2017). In mouse fibroblasts, human WI38 cells and Nrf2-knockout mice, rapamycin still lowered beta-galactosidase staining and the inflammatory secretory profile (SASP) without Nrf2, but needed Nrf2 to lower p16 and p21 and to switch on autophagy. The study pointed to lower STAT3 activation as one route for the SASP effect.

Wang published with the Pérez group at the Linus Pauling Institute from 2014 to 2022, on rapamycin and dietary restriction in mouse liver, rapamycin and bone in young adult mice, and senescence markers in the brains of Alzheimer's disease model mice. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.WAN2017: First author: showed in mouse and human fibroblasts and Nrf2-knockout mice that rapamycin lowers the senescence secretory profile without Nrf2 but needs Nrf2 to lower p16 and p21.

Perez VI.lab_name: Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging, NIH (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Perez VI.role: Aging biologist who studied protein homeostasis in long-lived species and how rapamycin and dietary restriction act in mice, and who now directs the National Institute on Aging's Division of Aging Biology
Perez VI.sub: Director, Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging · Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemistry & Biophysics, and Principal Investigator, Linus Pauling Institute, Oregon State University · postdoc, Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health Science Center at San Antonio (2004–2011) · PhD, University of Chile (2004)
story: Viviana Pérez was the senior author of the Atlas study in which her Oregon State group showed that rapamycin lowers the inflammatory secretory profile of senescent cells (SASP) without the transcription factor Nrf2, but needs Nrf2 to lower the cell-cycle brakes p16 and p21 (WAN2017). The work used mouse and human fibroblasts and a short dosing study in Nrf2-knockout mice.

Pérez trained as a pharmaceutical chemist and earned her PhD at the University of Chile, then spent seven years as a postdoctoral fellow at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, where she worked on oxidative stress and protein stability in long-lived species such as the naked mole-rat. At the Linus Pauling Institute her lab compared protein homeostasis in long- and short-lived species and tested whether rapamycin and dietary restriction act through the same mechanism in mice. She later moved to the National Institute on Aging, where she directs the Division of Aging Biology.

highlights.WAN2017: Senior author: led the study separating rapamycin's Nrf2-independent effect on the SASP from its Nrf2-dependent effect on p16 and p21.

Anisimov VN.lab_name: In memoriam / Department of Carcinogenesis and Oncogerontology, N.N. Petrov Research Institute of Oncology (St. Petersburg, Russia)
Anisimov VN.role: Russian gerontologist and oncologist who studied the links between ageing and cancer, and whose group tested drugs such as metformin and rapamycin for effects on lifespan and spontaneous tumours in mice
Anisimov VN.sub: Head, Department of Carcinogenesis and Oncogerontology (from 1999) and Laboratory of Carcinogenesis and Aging (from 1987), N.N. Petrov Research Institute of Oncology, St. Petersburg · Corresponding Member, Russian Academy of Sciences · President, Gerontological Society of the Russian Academy of Sciences · graduate, First Leningrad Medical Institute · 1945–2024
story: Vladimir Anisimov was first author of the Atlas study in which female 129/Sv inbred mice given rapamycin for two weeks of every month, from two months of age for life, gained less weight with age, lived longer and developed spontaneous tumours later (ANI2011). The paper, written with Mikhail Blagosklonny, extended earlier lifespan results from genetically heterogeneous mice to an intermittent schedule in a single inbred strain.

Born in Leningrad in 1945, Anisimov joined the N.N. Petrov Research Institute of Oncology in 1965 and spent his career there, heading its Laboratory of Carcinogenesis and Aging from 1987 and its Department of Carcinogenesis and Oncogerontology from 1999. He was a corresponding member of the Russian Academy of Sciences, president of the academy's Gerontological Society and editor of the journal Advances in Gerontology, and wrote several monographs and more than 400 research papers on ageing and cancer. He died in November 2024.

highlights.ANI2011: First author: showed that intermittent lifelong rapamycin extended lifespan and delayed spontaneous tumours in female 129/Sv inbred mice.

Fischer KE.lab_name: Department of Biology, University of Alabama at Birmingham (Birmingham, Alabama, USA)
Fischer KE.role: Comparative biologist of ageing who studies why ageing rates differ between sexes, strains and species, and who led a long-term study of how lifelong rapamycin affects health measures in mice
Fischer KE.sub: Research Adjunct Professor, Department of Biology, University of Alabama at Birmingham · Research Assistant Professor, Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health Science Center at San Antonio (2010–2014) · earlier conservation and natural-resource work (Wildlife Conservation Society; Yurok Tribe) · postdoc, Duke University (1998–1999) · PhD in Biology and Anthropology, Harvard University (1996)
story: Kathleen Fischer was first author of the Atlas study that fed C57BL/6J mice of both sexes rapamycin from four months of age until death and tested the same animals repeatedly for health measures from 16 months (FIS2015). Some measures improved, such as grip strength in females and sleep fragmentation in males, others did not change or got worse, and in body mass, fat and metabolic rate rapamycin moved males and females in opposite directions.

Fischer earned her PhD in biology and anthropology at Harvard and worked for several years in conservation and natural-resource management before returning to ageing research at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio. She moved to the University of Alabama at Birmingham in 2014, where she studies differences in ageing between sexes, strains and species with the aim of improving health in late life rather than lifespan alone.

highlights.FIS2015: First author: showed that lifelong dietary rapamycin in mice had mixed and strongly sex-specific effects on healthspan measures.

Austad SN.lab_name: Austad Lab, Department of Biology, University of Alabama at Birmingham (Birmingham, Alabama, USA)
Austad SN.role: Comparative biologist of ageing who studies why some species and one sex live longer than others, and who directs the UAB Nathan Shock Center; senior author of a study of how lifelong rapamycin affects health in mice
Austad SN.sub: Distinguished Professor and Protective Life Endowed Chair in Healthy Aging Research, Department of Biology, University of Alabama at Birmingham (since 2014) · Scientific Director, American Federation for Aging Research · Director, UAB Nathan Shock Center of Excellence in the Basic Biology of Aging · Professor, UT Health Science Center at San Antonio (2004–2013) · Professor, University of Idaho (1997–2004) · Harvard University faculty (1986–1992) · PhD, Purdue University (1981)
story: Steven Austad was the senior author of the Atlas study that followed mice fed rapamycin from four months of age until death and measured a broad panel of health measures from mid-life on (FIS2015). The study found that rapamycin improved some measures, left others unchanged and worsened a few, often in different directions in males and females.

Austad earned his PhD at Purdue and taught at Harvard and the University of Idaho before moving to the Barshop Institute in San Antonio in 2004 and to the University of Alabama at Birmingham in 2014. His work compares ageing across species, including long-lived animals, and between the sexes. He is scientific director of the American Federation for Aging Research and directs the UAB Nathan Shock Center of Excellence in the Basic Biology of Aging.

highlights.FIS2015: Senior author: lifelong rapamycin study in mice showing mixed and sex-specific effects on health measures.

Majumder S.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (affiliation on MAJ2012) (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Majumder S.role: First author of a mouse study in Salvatore Oddo's group showing that rapamycin started early in life, but not in middle age, protected against age-related memory decline
Majumder S.sub: Department of Physiology, UT Health Science Center at San Antonio (papers with Salvatore Oddo, 2009–2012)
story: Smita Majumder was first author of the Atlas study in which mice fed rapamycin from two months of age learned and remembered a water-maze task better at 18 months than untreated mice, while mice started on rapamycin at 15 months, when memory deficits were already present, did no better (MAJ2012). The early-treated mice had lower IL-1beta in the brain and higher phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit NR2B and of CREB.

Majumder published a series of papers with Salvatore Oddo's group at UT Health Science Center at San Antonio between 2009 and 2012 on mTOR, autophagy and memory in ageing and Alzheimer's disease model mice. No later institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAJ2012: First author: showed in mice that lifelong rapamycin from young adulthood, but not from middle age, protected spatial learning and memory at 18 months.

Yilmaz ÖH.lab_name: Yilmaz Lab, Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Department of Biology, MIT (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Yilmaz ÖH.role: Pathologist and stem-cell biologist who studies how diet and nutrient sensing control intestinal stem cells; as a postdoc with David Sabatini he showed that calorie restriction acts on the stem-cell niche through mTORC1 in Paneth cells
Yilmaz ÖH.sub: Associate Professor of Biology (tenured 2022), Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research, MIT · gastrointestinal pathologist, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School · own lab since 2014 · visiting postdoctoral fellow with David Sabatini, Whitehead Institute · thesis work with Sean Morrison, University of Michigan Medical School
story: Ömer Yilmaz was first author of the Atlas study showing in mice that calorie restriction increases intestinal stem-cell function by acting on the Paneth cells that form their niche (YIL2012). Restriction lowered mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells, forcing mTORC1 back on cancelled the effect, and a short course of rapamycin copied it; the niche signal ran through higher Bst1 and the messenger cyclic ADP ribose.

Yilmaz did his thesis work on blood stem cells with Sean Morrison at the University of Michigan and then spent two years as a visiting postdoctoral fellow in David Sabatini's lab, where the Atlas study was done. He started his own lab at MIT's Koch Institute in 2014 and also works as a gastrointestinal pathologist at Massachusetts General Hospital. His group studies how diet, including fasting and high-fat diets, changes intestinal stem cells and the early steps of colon cancer.

highlights.YIL2012: First author: showed in mice that calorie restriction boosts intestinal stem cells by lowering mTORC1 in their Paneth-cell niche.

Pearce EL.lab_name: Pearce Lab, Department of Oncology and Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Johns Hopkins University (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Pearce EL.role: Immunologist who studies how metabolism controls T-cell fate. As a postdoc at Penn she showed in mice that drugs that raise fatty acid oxidation, metformin and rapamycin, increase CD8 memory T cells
Pearce EL.sub: Bloomberg Distinguished Professor, Johns Hopkins University (Department of Oncology, School of Medicine; Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Biology, Bloomberg School of Public Health) · Director, Department of Immunometabolism, Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics, Freiburg (from 2015) · Assistant then Associate Professor, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis (2011–2015) · Trudeau Institute (2009–2011) · PhD (2005) and postdoc, University of Pennsylvania · Leibniz Prize (2018)
story: Erika Pearce was first author of the Atlas study showing that mouse CD8 T cells lacking the adaptor TRAF6 failed to switch on AMPK and fatty acid oxidation and so formed almost no memory cells, and that daily metformin restored memory formation (PEA2009). Rapamycin, used as a second drug that promotes fatty acid oxidation, also increased memory CD8 T cells. The paper appeared in the same issue of Nature as a study from Rafi Ahmed's group reporting that rapamycin enhances memory CD8 T cells.

Pearce earned her PhD in cell and molecular biology at the University of Pennsylvania and stayed at Penn for postdoctoral work, where she began studying how metabolism shapes immune responses. She started her own lab at the Trudeau Institute, moved to Washington University in St. Louis, and in 2015 became a director at the Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics in Freiburg. She then moved to Johns Hopkins as a Bloomberg Distinguished Professor, where her group studies how mitochondrial structure and metabolism control T-cell differentiation, survival and function.

highlights.PEA2009: First author: showed in mice that boosting fatty acid oxidation with metformin or rapamycin increases CD8 memory T-cell formation.

Choi Y.lab_name: Choi Lab, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Choi Y.role: Immunologist who studies TRAF6 and RANKL (TRANCE) signalling at the junction of the immune and skeletal systems; senior author of the study linking TRAF6 and fatty acid oxidation to CD8 T-cell memory
Choi Y.sub: Leonard Jarett Professor of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · research fellow with John Kappler and Philippa Marrack, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, National Jewish Center for Immunology and Respiratory Medicine, Denver (1988–1992) · PhD in Biochemistry, University of Illinois College of Medicine, Chicago (1988) · BSc, Seoul National University (1984)
story: Yongwon Choi was the senior author of the Atlas study in which mouse CD8 T cells lacking the adaptor protein TRAF6 mounted a normal effector response but formed almost no memory cells, because they could not switch on AMPK and fatty acid oxidation (PEA2009). Metformin restored memory formation, and rapamycin, used as a second drug that promotes fatty acid oxidation, also increased memory CD8 T cells.

Choi earned his PhD at the University of Illinois College of Medicine and trained with John Kappler and Philippa Marrack in Denver. His lab at the University of Pennsylvania works on osteoimmunology, the cross-talk between bone metabolism and the immune system, including how TRAF6 transmits IL-1, Toll-like receptor and RANKL signals, how dendritic cells and bone-resorbing osteoclasts differentiate, and how T-cell tolerance is maintained.

highlights.PEA2009: Senior author: TRAF6-deficient CD8 T cells failed to form memory, which metformin or rapamycin restored by raising fatty acid oxidation.

Rao RR.lab_name: Shrikant Lab, Department of Immunology, Roswell Park Cancer Institute (affiliation on RAO2010) (Buffalo, New York, USA)
Rao RR.role: First author of mouse studies in Protul Shrikant's group showing that mTOR activity decides between effector and memory fates in CD8 T cells by controlling T-bet and Eomesodermin
Rao RR.sub: Department of Immunology, Roswell Park Cancer Institute, Buffalo (papers with Protul Shrikant, 2010–2012)
story: Rajesh Rao was first author of the Atlas study in which IL-12 raised and prolonged mTOR activity in naive mouse CD8 T cells, and rapamycin blocked sustained T-bet expression, raised Eomesodermin and produced memory-precursor cells that persisted and controlled tumours better after transfer (RAO2010). A 2012 follow-up from the same group, also with Rao as first author, placed the transcription factor Foxo1 downstream of mTORC1 in this switch. The 2010 paper appeared in the same period as studies from other groups linking mTOR inhibition by rapamycin to better CD8 T-cell memory.
PubMed gives his forename as Rajesh. No current institutional page was found that can be tied to this person with confidence, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RAO2010: First author: showed in mouse CD8 T cells that sustained mTOR activity drives T-bet and effector fate, while rapamycin favours Eomesodermin and memory precursors.

Shrikant PA.lab_name: Shrikant Lab, Department of Immunobiology, University of Arizona College of Medicine (Tucson, Arizona, USA)
Shrikant PA.role: Tumour immunologist whose Roswell Park group showed in mouse CD8 T cells that mTOR activity, driven by IL-12, decides between effector and memory fates through T-bet and Eomesodermin
Shrikant PA.sub: Professor of Immunobiology, University of Arizona College of Medicine, Tucson · earlier faculty, Department of Immunology, Roswell Park Cancer Institute, Buffalo (affiliation on RAO2010) · postdoc with Matthew Mescher, Center for Immunology, University of Minnesota (1996–2000) · PhD, University of Alabama at Birmingham (1995)
story: Protul Shrikant was the senior author of the Atlas study showing that IL-12 sustains mTOR activity in antigen-stimulated mouse CD8 T cells, that this keeps T-bet switched on for effector function, and that blocking mTOR with rapamycin raises Eomesodermin and produces memory-precursor cells with better persistence and tumour control after transfer (RAO2010). Follow-up work from his group linked mTOR to homeostatic proliferation of CD8 T cells and to the transcription factor Foxo1.

Shrikant earned his PhD at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and did postdoctoral work on CD8 T-cell responses to tumours with Matthew Mescher at the University of Minnesota. He then led a group in the Department of Immunology at Roswell Park Cancer Institute in Buffalo, and is now Professor of Immunobiology at the University of Arizona, where his research focuses on anti-tumour immunity.

highlights.RAO2010: Senior author: identified mTOR as the switch between effector and memory programmes in mouse CD8 T cells via T-bet and Eomesodermin.

Michalek RD.role: T-cell metabolism researcher who, as a postdoc with Jeffrey Rathmell, showed that effector CD4 T cells rely on glycolysis while regulatory T cells rely on lipid oxidation, which ties the pro-Treg effect of rapamycin to fatty acid oxidation; he later moved into metabolomics in industry
Michalek RD.sub: Senior Study Director, Metabolon, Inc., Durham · postdoc with Jeffrey Rathmell, Department of Pharmacology & Cancer Biology, Duke University
story: Ryan Michalek was first author of the Atlas study showing that Th1, Th2 and Th17 cells carry high levels of the glucose transporter Glut1 and are strongly glycolytic, while inducible regulatory T cells carry little Glut1, have active AMPK and oxidise lipid (MIC2011). Blocking lipid oxidation selectively suppressed Treg generation and prevented the Treg increase produced by rapamycin, linking the pro-Treg effect of mTOR inhibition to fatty acid oxidation in these mouse cells.

Michalek did this work as a postdoctoral fellow in Jeffrey Rathmell's lab at Duke University. He then joined Metabolon, a metabolomics company in North Carolina, where he has co-authored metabolomic studies with academic groups; the Rathmell lab's alumni page lists him as a senior study director there.

highlights.MIC2011: First author: showed in mouse CD4 T cells that effector subsets are glycolytic while Treg depend on lipid oxidation, which rapamycin's pro-Treg effect requires.

Rathmell JC.lab_name: Rathmell Lab, Ben May Department for Cancer Research, University of Chicago (Chicago, Illinois, USA)
Rathmell JC.role: Studies how nutrients and metabolic pathways control lymphocyte growth, differentiation and function; his lab helped show that effector and regulatory CD4 T cells rely on different fuel programmes, glycolysis versus lipid oxidation (in mouse cells).
Rathmell JC.sub: Chair, Ben May Department for Cancer Research, Virginia and D. K. Ludwig Chair Professor and Director, Ludwig Center for Metastasis Research, University of Chicago (since 2025) · Cornelius Vanderbilt Professor of Immunobiology and Director, Vanderbilt Center for Immunobiology, Vanderbilt University Medical Center (2015–2025) · faculty, Duke University (2003–2015) · postdoc with Craig B. Thompson, University of Chicago and University of Pennsylvania · PhD in immunology, Stanford University
story: Jeffrey Rathmell was senior author of the 2011 Journal of Immunology study (MIC2011) comparing the metabolism of mouse CD4 T cells grown as effector (Th1, Th2, Th17) or induced regulatory cells. Effector cells carried a lot of the glucose transporter Glut1 and were strongly glycolytic, while regulatory cells oxidised more lipid and had more active AMPK. Blocking lipid oxidation with etomoxir suppressed regulatory T-cell generation and also prevented the rise in regulatory cells caused by rapamycin, which links the pro-regulatory effect of mTOR inhibition to lipid oxidation. mTOR activity itself was not measured; the mTOR step rests on the drug effects.

Rathmell earned his PhD in immunology at Stanford University and did postdoctoral work with Craig B. Thompson at the University of Chicago and the University of Pennsylvania. He started his own lab at Duke University in 2003, moved to Vanderbilt in 2015 to direct the Vanderbilt Center for Immunobiology, and in July 2025 became chair of the Ben May Department for Cancer Research at the University of Chicago. His lab works on how nutrient environments, for example in obesity or inflamed tissue, shape immune-cell metabolism and cancer immunotherapy.

highlights.MIC2011: Senior author: effector CD4 T cells are glycolytic while regulatory T cells depend on lipid oxidation, which also underlies the rapamycin-driven increase in regulatory cells (mouse cells).

Marcais A.lab_name: NK cell immunometabolism group, LYACTS team, Centre International de Recherche en Infectiologie (CIRI), INSERM / ENS de Lyon (Lyon, France)
Marcais A.role: Studies how mTOR and cell metabolism control natural killer (NK) cells; first author of the mouse study showing that NK cells need mTOR to respond to IL-15 during their development and activation.
Marcais A.sub: Group leader, NK cell immunometabolism, LYACTS team (Thierry Walzer), CIRI, Lyon · earlier work on CD8 T cells at INSERM U503, Lyon (mid-2000s)
story: Antoine Marçais was first author of the 2014 Nature Immunology study (MAR2014) from Thierry Walzer's team. It showed that low IL-15 mainly switches on STAT5 in NK cells while higher IL-15 is needed to switch on mTOR, and that mice whose NK cells lack mTOR have almost no mature NK cells in the periphery. mTOR-deficient NK cells also failed to grow and to make normal amounts of granzyme B after activation, and oral rapamycin made NK-cell rejection of target cells less efficient. Human data in the paper are limited to NK cells from healthy donors stimulated in culture.

Marçais now leads the NK cell immunometabolism group inside the LYACTS team at CIRI in Lyon, which asks how mTOR, glycolysis and NK-cell reactivity are linked and why mTOR activation is impaired in exhausted NK cells. He supervised the PhD of Lucie Fallone on how IL-15 and IL-18 regulate the mTOR pathway in NK cells (defended 2024).

highlights.MAR2014: First author: NK cells need mTOR, switched on by high-dose IL-15, to mature and to become fully activated (mouse genetics, plus human NK cells in culture).

Walzer T.lab_name: LYACTS team (Walzer lab), Centre International de Recherche en Infectiologie (CIRI), INSERM / ENS de Lyon (Lyon, France)
Walzer T.role: Studies how natural killer (NK) cells develop and become active; his team showed in mice that IL-15 signalling through mTOR is needed for NK-cell maturation and activation.
Walzer T.sub: Team leader, CIRI, Lyon (since 2009) · principal investigator in Eric Vivier's laboratory, Centre d'Immunologie de Marseille-Luminy (2004–2009) · postdoc, Amgen, Seattle (2002–2004) · PhD with Jacqueline Marvel, ENS de Lyon (1999–2002)
story: Thierry Walzer was senior author of the 2014 Nature Immunology study (MAR2014) that separated two arms of IL-15 signalling in NK cells by dose: STAT5 at low IL-15 and mTOR at higher IL-15. Mice whose NK cells lack mTOR had normal numbers of NK cells in the bone marrow but almost none that were mature in the periphery, and mTOR-deficient NK cells made about half the normal granzyme B after activation. Rapamycin given by mouth reduced NK-cell killing of target cells in mice; the possible effect on patients taking rapalogs is an inference, not a measured outcome.

Walzer did his PhD on memory CD8 T cells with Jacqueline Marvel at the École Normale Supérieure de Lyon, worked as a postdoc at Amgen in Seattle, and then ran a group on NK cells and innate immunity in Eric Vivier's laboratory in Marseille. Since 2009 he has led a team at CIRI in Lyon, now called LYACTS, which works on NK-cell differentiation and reactivity, NK-cell immunometabolism and the genetics of early-onset autoimmunity.

highlights.MAR2014: Senior author: high-dose IL-15 switches on mTOR in NK cells, and mTOR is needed for NK-cell maturation and full activation (mouse genetics, plus human NK cells in culture).

Bensinger SJ.lab_name: Bensinger Lab, Department of Immunology and Immune Therapeutics, Keck School of Medicine of USC (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Bensinger SJ.role: Studies how lipid metabolism shapes innate and adaptive immunity; his lab showed in mice that activated CD8 T cells need SREBP-driven cholesterol and fatty-acid synthesis, switched on through mTOR, in order to grow and divide.
Bensinger SJ.sub: Chair, Department of Immunology and Immune Therapeutics, Keck School of Medicine of USC (since 2025) · Professor and Vice Chair for Academic Personnel, Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Molecular Genetics, and Director, UCLA Lipidomics Laboratory, UCLA · postdoc with Peter Tontonoz, UCLA · PhD in immunology with Laurence Turka, University of Pennsylvania · VMD
story: Steven Bensinger was senior author of the 2013 Nature Immunology study (KID2013), done at UCLA. Activated mouse T cells switch on cholesterol and fatty-acid synthesis genes within hours, and rapamycin given before stimulation blocked this programme and the processing of the transcription factors SREBP1 and SREBP2. T cells lacking SREBP activity (Scap deletion) could not grow into blasts after activation, and adding cholesterol restored their growth, pointing to cholesterol as the limiting step. In infected mice, these cells produced a weaker virus-specific CD8 T-cell response.

Bensinger trained in veterinary medicine and did his PhD in immunology with Laurence Turka at the University of Pennsylvania, working on regulatory T cells, and then a postdoc with Peter Tontonoz at UCLA on lipid metabolism and T-cell growth. He built his own lab at UCLA, where he directed the UCLA Lipidomics Laboratory, and in September 2025 became chair of the Department of Immunology and Immune Therapeutics at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

highlights.KID2013: Senior author: mTOR-dependent SREBP activity supplies the cholesterol activated CD8 T cells need to grow and expand (mouse genetics and mouse cells).

Geiger R.lab_name: Systems Immunology group, Institute for Research in Biomedicine (IRB), Università della Svizzera italiana (Bellinzona, Switzerland)
Geiger R.role: Studies how metabolism regulates T-cell responses against tumours; first author of the study showing that raising L-arginine shifts human T cells towards oxidative metabolism and longer survival, an effect the authors found to be independent of mTOR.
Geiger R.sub: Group leader, Systems Immunology, IRB Bellinzona (since 2017), and Associate Professor, USI · proteomics training in Matthias Mann's group, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Munich (2016) · SystemsX postdoc with Antonio Lanzavecchia, IRB Bellinzona (from 2011) · MSc and PhD (with Ari Helenius), ETH Zurich
story: Roger Geiger was first author of the 2016 Cell study (GEI2016) from Antonio Lanzavecchia's lab. Activated human T cells use up their intracellular L-arginine quickly; adding more shifted them from glycolysis towards oxidative phosphorylation and produced central-memory-like cells that survived longer. Three nuclear proteins (BAZ1B, PSIP1 and TSN) were identified as L-arginine sensors. In mice, L-arginine-treated T cells slowed the growth of a transplanted melanoma. The authors report that this survival effect did not go through mTOR: L-arginine did not change S6K1 or 4E-BP phosphorylation, and mTOR enters the paper only as a comparison.

Geiger did his master's and PhD at ETH Zurich, the PhD with Ari Helenius on how non-enveloped viruses cross cell membranes. He joined Lanzavecchia's lab at IRB in 2011 as a SystemsX postdoc, trained in mass-spectrometry proteomics with Matthias Mann in Munich in 2016, and started his own Systems Immunology group at IRB in 2017. He received an ERC Starting Grant and joined the EMBO Young Investigator Programme in 2022.

highlights.GEI2016: First author: higher L-arginine makes activated human T cells more oxidative, more memory-like and longer-lived, through nuclear sensors rather than mTOR (human cells in culture, mouse tumour models).

Lanzavecchia A.lab_name: Lanzavecchia Lab, Human Immunology Program, Istituto Nazionale di Genetica Molecolare (INGM) (Milan, Italy)
Lanzavecchia A.role: Human immunologist known for work on antigen presentation, memory T and B cells and methods for isolating human monoclonal antibodies; senior author of the study showing that L-arginine changes T-cell metabolism and survival independently of mTOR.
Lanzavecchia A.sub: Head, Human Immunology Program, INGM, Milan, and Senior Research Fellow, Vir Biotechnology · founding Director, Institute for Research in Biomedicine, Bellinzona (until 2020) · Professor of Human Immunology, ETH Zurich (2009–2017) · member, Basel Institute for Immunology (from 1983) · MD, University of Pavia (1976), with specialisation in paediatrics and infectious diseases
story: Antonio Lanzavecchia was senior author of the 2016 Cell study (GEI2016) in which his group, with Roger Geiger as first author, tracked metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells. Raising L-arginine moved the cells from glycolysis towards oxidative phosphorylation, gave them central-memory-like features and better survival, and improved their anti-tumour activity in mice. The paper states that this effect was independent of mTOR, since L-arginine did not change S6K1 or 4E-BP phosphorylation and rapamycin changed metabolism in a different way.

Lanzavecchia studied medicine at the University of Pavia and specialised in paediatrics and infectious diseases. He worked at the University of Genoa and then at the Basel Institute for Immunology, and was the founding director of the Institute for Research in Biomedicine in Bellinzona. He is the scientific founder of Humabs BioMed, now part of Vir Biotechnology, where he is a senior research fellow, and his academic research continues at INGM in Milan. He is an international member of the US National Academy of Sciences (2016).

highlights.GEI2016: Senior author: L-arginine shifts activated human T cells towards oxidative metabolism and longer survival, through nuclear sensors and not through mTOR (human cells in culture, mouse tumour models).

Tang SJ.lab_name: Tang Lab, Department of Anesthesiology, Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University (Stony Brook, New York, USA)
Tang SJ.role: Neuroscientist who, as a postdoc in Erin Schuman's group at Caltech, helped show that a rapamycin-sensitive mTOR pathway is needed for the protein-synthesis-dependent late phase of hippocampal LTP; his lab now studies chronic pain.
Tang SJ.sub: Stony Brook Medicine Endowed Professor in Anesthesiology, Vice Chair for Research and Director, Stony Brook University Pain and Analgesia Research Center · earlier Cecil H. and Ida M. Green Distinguished Chair in Neuroscience and Cell Biology, University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston · postdoc in synaptic plasticity, Caltech / HHMI, Pasadena · MS and PhD, University of Toronto
story: Shao-Jun Tang was first author of the PNAS paper (TAN2002; published online in December 2001) from Erin Schuman's group at Caltech. It showed that mTOR, 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2 and eIF4E sit in the dendrites of rat hippocampal neurons, close to synapses, and that rapamycin reduces the late, protein-synthesis-dependent phase of long-term potentiation while leaving the early phase intact. Rapamycin also blocked the synaptic strengthening caused by the growth factor BDNF. The work was done in rodent brain slices and cultured neurons.

Tang trained in molecular genetics at the University of Toronto and did his postdoctoral work on synaptic plasticity at Caltech, in a Howard Hughes Medical Institute group. He later held the Cecil H. and Ida M. Green Distinguished Chair in Neuroscience and Cell Biology at the University of Texas Medical Branch and now directs the Pain and Analgesia Research Center at Stony Brook University.

highlights.TAN2002: First author: rapamycin reduces late-phase LTP and BDNF-induced potentiation, and mTOR pathway proteins sit at synapses (rat hippocampal slices and neurons).

Schuman EM.lab_name: Department of Synaptic Plasticity, Max Planck Institute for Brain Research (Frankfurt am Main, Germany)
Schuman EM.role: Studies how neurons make and break down proteins locally in dendrites and axons; her group helped tie a rapamycin-sensitive mTOR pathway to the protein-synthesis-dependent phase of synaptic plasticity.
Schuman EM.sub: Director, Max Planck Institute for Brain Research, Frankfurt (since 2009) · Professor, Goethe University Frankfurt · Assistant to Full Professor of Biology, Caltech (1993–2010), and HHMI Investigator · postdoc, Stanford University (Daniel Madison lab, 1990–1993) · PhD in neuroscience, Princeton University (1990)
story: Erin Schuman was senior author of the PNAS study (TAN2002), with Shao-Jun Tang as first author and Nahum Sonenberg's lab as collaborator. Her group found mTOR, the 4E-BPs and eIF4E in the dendrites of rat hippocampal neurons near synapses, and showed that rapamycin reduces late-phase long-term potentiation and BDNF-induced potentiation without affecting early-phase LTP. This was one of the early papers to link an mTOR-dependent translation pathway to synaptic plasticity and local protein synthesis at synapses.

Schuman did her PhD in neuroscience at Princeton and a postdoc with Daniel Madison at Stanford, then spent 1993–2010 on the Caltech biology faculty, where she was also a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator. Since 2009 she has been a director at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, where her department studies the mRNAs and ribosomes found in dendrites and axons and how local protein synthesis and degradation shape synapses. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences (2020) and received The Brain Prize in 2023.

highlights.TAN2002: Senior author: rapamycin-sensitive mTOR signalling is needed for late-phase LTP and BDNF-induced potentiation in rat hippocampus, and its components sit at synapses.

Gkogkas CG.lab_name: Gkogkas Lab, Biomedical Research Institute, Foundation for Research and Technology – Hellas (FORTH) (Ioannina, Greece)
Gkogkas CG.role: Studies how protein synthesis is controlled in the brain; first author of the mouse study linking loss of the translational repressor 4E-BP2, downstream of mTORC1, to autism-like behaviour through increased neuroligin translation.
Gkogkas CG.sub: Research Director, Biomedical Research Institute, FORTH, Ioannina (since 2023; principal investigator since 2019) · Chancellor's Fellow, University of Edinburgh, Centre for Discovery Brain Sciences and Patrick Wild Centre (2013–2019) · postdoc with Nahum Sonenberg, McGill University (2009–2013) · PhD in molecular neuroscience, University of Edinburgh (2009)
story: Christos Gkogkas was first author of the 2013 Nature study (GKO2013) from Nahum Sonenberg's lab at McGill. Mice lacking 4E-BP2, the main brake on eIF4E in the brain downstream of mTORC1, showed autism-like behaviours and a higher ratio of excitatory to inhibitory synaptic activity. Of 24 autism-linked mRNAs tested, only the neuroligin mRNAs were translated more, and blocking eIF4E with the drug 4EGI-1 or reducing neuroligin 1 restored social behaviour. The work is in mice; mTOR itself was not manipulated, and the link to human autism is by analogy.

Gkogkas studied biology in Athens and did his MSc and PhD at the University of Edinburgh, then a postdoc with Nahum Sonenberg at McGill University (2009–2013). He returned to Edinburgh as a Chancellor's Fellow in 2013 and since 2019 has led a group at the FORTH Biomedical Research Institute in Ioannina, Greece, which studies translational control in the brain using brain organoids and rodent disease models.

highlights.GKO2013: First author: loss of 4E-BP2 increases neuroligin translation and causes autism-like behaviour in mice, reversed by blocking eIF4E.

Cota D.lab_name: Energy Balance and Obesity team, Neurocentre Magendie, INSERM U1215, University of Bordeaux (Bordeaux, France)
Cota D.role: Studies how the brain senses nutrients and hormones to control food intake and body weight; as a postdoc in Cincinnati she was first author of the rat study that tied hypothalamic mTOR signalling to food intake and leptin action.
Cota D.sub: INSERM Research Director (DR2) and leader, Energy Balance and Obesity team, Neurocentre Magendie, Bordeaux · Deputy Director, Neurocentre Magendie · postdoc with Randy Seeley and Stephen Woods, University of Cincinnati (2004–2007) · postdoc, Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry, Munich (2001–2003) · MD and specialisation in endocrinology, University of Bologna
story: Daniela Cota was first author of the 2006 Science study (COT2006). Working in rats, the team found that mTOR signalling in the hypothalamus, read out as phosphorylated S6K1 and S6, changed with the animal's energy status and was present in NPY and POMC neurons of the arcuate nucleus. Leucine injected into the brain raised hypothalamic mTOR signalling and lowered food intake and body weight, and leptin also raised mTOR activity; blocking mTOR with rapamycin in the brain blunted leptin's effect on eating. The authors proposed that hypothalamic mTOR acts as a fuel sensor. These are short-term results in rats with direct brain dosing.

Cota trained in medicine and endocrinology at the University of Bologna, then worked at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich and, from 2004 to 2007, in the University of Cincinnati groups of Randy Seeley and Stephen Woods. She set up an INSERM team in Bordeaux in 2008 and now leads the Energy Balance and Obesity team at the Neurocentre Magendie, whose work includes mTORC1 and mTORC2 signalling in POMC neurons and the endocannabinoid system in energy balance.

highlights.COT2006: First author: in rats, hypothalamic mTOR signalling tracks energy status, leucine in the brain lowers food intake, and rapamycin blunts leptin's effect on eating.

Seeley RJ.lab_name: Seeley Lab, Department of Surgery, University of Michigan Medical School (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Seeley RJ.role: Studies how gut and brain signals control appetite, body weight and blood sugar, including why bariatric surgery works; his Cincinnati lab was senior on the rat study linking hypothalamic mTOR to food intake.
Seeley RJ.sub: Henry King Ransom Endowed Professor of Surgery, University of Michigan (since 2014) · previously Professor of Medicine and Donald C. Harrison Endowed Chair, and Director of the Cincinnati Diabetes and Obesity Center, University of Cincinnati (from 1997) · postdoc, University of Washington (1993–1995) · PhD in psychology, University of Pennsylvania (1993)
story: Randy Seeley was senior author of the 2006 Science study led by Daniela Cota (COT2006). In rats, hypothalamic mTOR signalling changed with energy status, central leucine raised it and reduced food intake and body weight, and inhibiting mTOR with rapamycin blunted the appetite-lowering effect of leptin. The work suggested that hypothalamic mTOR acts as a nutrient sensor that feeds into the control of eating, in rats.

Seeley trained in psychology at Grinnell College and the University of Pennsylvania and did a postdoc at the University of Washington. He spent about 17 years at the University of Cincinnati, where he directed the Cincinnati Diabetes and Obesity Center, and moved to the University of Michigan in 2014. His lab studies gut-brain signalling, bariatric surgery and metabolism, including hormones such as GLP-1 and leptin and the bile-acid receptor FXR.

highlights.COT2006: Senior author: hypothalamic mTOR signalling responds to energy status and leucine, and is needed for leptin's full effect on food intake in rats.

Tsai PT.lab_name: Tsai Lab, Department of Neurology, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Tsai PT.role: Child neurologist and neuroscientist who studies how the cerebellum contributes to autism; first author of the mouse study showing that loss of Tsc1 in Purkinje cells causes autism-like behaviour that rapamycin can prevent.
Tsai PT.sub: Associate Professor of Neurology, Neuroscience, Pediatrics and Psychiatry, UT Southwestern Medical Center · earlier Instructor in Neurology, Harvard Medical School / Boston Children's Hospital · pediatrics and child neurology residencies and behavioural neurology fellowship, Boston Children's Hospital (to 2011) · MD/PhD, David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (2005)
story: Peter Tsai was first author of the 2012 Nature study from Mustafa Sahin's group at Boston Children's Hospital (TSA2012). Deleting one or both copies of Tsc1 only in cerebellar Purkinje cells raised mTORC1 activity in those cells and produced autism-like behaviour in mice: reduced social preference, more self-grooming, more pup calls and poorer reversal learning. Purkinje cells fired less, homozygous mutants lost Purkinje cells and became ataxic, and rapamycin started from postnatal day 7 prevented these changes. This is prevention in mice; links to human autism are by analogy with tuberous sclerosis complex.

Tsai earned an MD/PhD at UCLA and trained in pediatrics, child neurology and behavioural neurology at Boston Children's Hospital, where he was an instructor at Harvard Medical School at the time of the study. He moved to UT Southwestern in Dallas, where his lab studies synapse and circuit development and cerebellar contributions to cognition and behaviour, and he sees patients at the Center for Autism and Neurodevelopmental Disabilities.

highlights.TSA2012: First author: mice lacking Tsc1 in cerebellar Purkinje cells show autism-like behaviour and Purkinje cell dysfunction, prevented by early rapamycin.
highlights.LIP2017: Co-author of the Sahin-lab follow-up on how mTORC1 shapes the daily (circadian) clock through BMAL1; Mustafa Sahin was senior author.

Sabatini BL.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Sabatini BL.role: Neurobiologist who studies how synapses and circuits change during development and learning; his lab showed that loss of Tsc1 in mouse hippocampal neurons weakens inhibitory input and tips circuits toward hyperexcitability.
Sabatini BL.sub: Alice and Rodman W. Moorhead III Professor of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School · HHMI Investigator (since 2008) · Co-director, Kempner Institute, Harvard · joined HMS faculty 2001 · postdoc with Karel Svoboda, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory · MD (Harvard–MIT HST, 1999) and PhD (Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School)
story: Bernardo Sabatini was senior author of the 2013 Neuron study led by Helen Bateup (BAT2013). Deleting Tsc1 in cultured mouse hippocampal neurons more than doubled network activity, and rapamycin brought it back to normal; many molecular changes in these cultures turned out to be responses to the extra activity rather than direct effects of mTOR. In hippocampal slices, single neurons lacking Tsc1 received weaker inhibitory input, which raised their excitation/inhibition ratio, and forebrain Tsc1 knockout mice had more severe chemically induced seizures. Seven days of rapamycin restored inhibition. The work is in mouse neurons and brain slices.

Bernardo Sabatini (not the mTOR biochemist David M. Sabatini, who has his own profile) trained in the Harvard–MIT MD/PhD programme and did a postdoc with Karel Svoboda at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. He joined Harvard Medical School in 2001; his lab uses optical methods, slice physiology and behaving mice to study cortex, hippocampus and basal ganglia, with an interest in circuit changes linked to autism and Parkinson's disease.

highlights.BAT2013: Senior author: Tsc1 loss in mouse hippocampal neurons weakens inhibition and causes network hyperexcitability that rapamycin reverses.

Atkins MB.lab_name: Georgetown Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, Georgetown University Medical Center (Washington, District of Columbia, USA)
Atkins MB.role: Medical oncologist specialising in kidney cancer and melanoma; led the randomised phase II dose study of temsirolimus (CCI-779) in advanced kidney cancer that supported taking the 25 mg weekly dose forward.
Atkins MB.sub: Deputy Director, Georgetown Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Scholl Professor and Vice Chair, Department of Medical Oncology, Georgetown University Medical Center (at Georgetown since 2014) · previously Professor of Medicine and Deputy Chief of Hematology/Oncology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School, and leader of the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center kidney cancer program · MD, Tufts University School of Medicine (1980)
story: Michael Atkins was first author of the 2004 Journal of Clinical Oncology trial (ATK2004). 111 patients with advanced kidney cancer that had progressed on earlier treatment were randomised to weekly intravenous temsirolimus at 25, 75 or 250 mg. The objective response rate was 7%, median time to progression 5.8 months and median survival 15.0 months; efficacy and toxicity did not differ clearly between doses, which supported the lowest dose. There was no placebo or comparator arm, so survival figures cannot be attributed to the drug.

Atkins trained at Tufts and spent much of his career at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, where he led the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center kidney cancer program and its kidney cancer SPORE. He moved to Georgetown in 2014 as deputy director of the Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, where he co-directs the melanoma programme and leads kidney cancer research.

highlights.ATK2004: First author: in a randomised phase II dose study, temsirolimus gave a 7% response rate in refractory kidney cancer with no clear difference between 25, 75 and 250 mg.

Sherman ML.role: Oncologist and drug developer who led clinical programmes at Wyeth, including the sponsor side of the phase II temsirolimus (CCI-779) dose study in kidney cancer.
Sherman ML.sub: Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer, Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (since 2019) · earlier Chief Medical Officer, Acceleron Pharma, and Senior Vice President and Chief Medical Officer, Synta Pharmaceuticals · more than a decade at Wyeth-Ayerst Research / Genetics Institute · medical oncology fellowship, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute · MD, Dartmouth Medical School
story: Matthew Sherman was senior author, on the sponsor side at Wyeth, of the 2004 randomised phase II trial of temsirolimus (CCI-779) in advanced, previously treated kidney cancer (ATK2004). Patients received 25, 75 or 250 mg weekly; the response rate was 7% and neither efficacy nor toxicity differed clearly by dose, which supported the 25 mg dose used later. The trial had no control arm.

Sherman trained in chemistry at MIT, in medicine at Dartmouth, in internal medicine at Georgetown and in medical oncology at Dana-Farber, and held academic posts at Harvard Medical School. He spent more than ten years at Wyeth-Ayerst Research and Genetics Institute, where he also worked on the antibody-drug conjugate gemtuzumab ozogamicin for acute myeloid leukaemia, and later served as chief medical officer at Synta Pharmaceuticals, Acceleron Pharma and Deciphera Pharmaceuticals.

highlights.ATK2004: Senior author (Wyeth): randomised phase II dose study of temsirolimus in refractory kidney cancer that supported the 25 mg weekly dose.

Crone KR.lab_name: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Cincinnati College of Medicine (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Crone KR.role: Pediatric neurosurgeon in Cincinnati; senior author of the small case series in which oral rapamycin shrank brain astrocytomas in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex.
Crone KR.sub: Physician and Residency Associate Program Director, Department of Neurosurgery, University of Cincinnati College of Medicine · Clinical Scholar in neurosurgery, Children's Hospital Medical Center, Cincinnati (1986) · pediatric neurosurgery fellowship, Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto (1986) · neurosurgery residency, North Carolina Baptist Hospital · MD, University of Cincinnati (1978)
story: Kerry Crone was senior author of the 2006 Annals of Neurology report led by David Franz (FRA2006). Five people with tuberous sclerosis complex whose brain astrocytomas were growing were treated with oral rapamycin at standard immunosuppressive blood levels. Every lesion shrank on MRI, and in one patient the tumour regrew when treatment stopped and shrank again when it restarted. This was an uncontrolled series of five patients, one of the early clinical reports that came before the EXIST-1 everolimus trial and the authors suggested that the drug might offer an alternative to surgery for these tumours.

Crone studied medicine at the University of Cincinnati, trained in neurosurgery at North Carolina Baptist Hospital and in pediatric neurosurgery at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, and was a clinical scholar in neurosurgery at Children's Hospital Medical Center, Cincinnati, in 1986. He is listed in the University of Cincinnati Department of Neurosurgery.

highlights.FRA2006: Senior author: oral rapamycin shrank growing TSC-associated brain astrocytomas in all five treated patients, with regrowth when treatment was interrupted.

Zeng LH.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Novel Targets and Drug Study for Neural Repair of Zhejiang Province, School of Medicine, Hangzhou City University (Hangzhou, China)
Zeng LH.role: Pharmacologist who studies mTOR signalling in epilepsy; as a researcher in Michael Wong's group she was first author of the mouse study showing that rapamycin prevents epilepsy in a tuberous sclerosis model.
Zeng LH.sub: School of Medicine, Hangzhou City University (formerly Zhejiang University City College), Hangzhou · earlier Department of Neurology, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis (about 2007–2008, with Michael Wong)
story: Ling-Hui Zeng was first author of the 2008 Annals of Neurology study from Michael Wong's group (ZEN2008). Mice lacking Tsc1 mainly in glial cells develop progressive epilepsy and die early. Rapamycin started at postnatal day 14 prevented the epilepsy and early death, and rapamycin started at 6 weeks, after seizures had begun, suppressed seizures and prolonged survival. It also reversed raised phospho-S6, astrogliosis and neuronal disorganisation. The results are from a mouse model, not patients, and they are part of the background to the later EXIST-3 trial (FRE2016).

Zeng worked in the Department of Neurology at Washington University in St. Louis in the mid-2000s, on the same Tsc1 glial knockout mouse. She then moved to Hangzhou, to Zhejiang University City College, now Hangzhou City University, where her group has continued to publish on mTOR in seizures, including rat studies on the timing and dose of rapamycin, and more recently on other neural and tumour signalling pathways.

highlights.ZEN2008: First author: in Tsc1 glial knockout mice, early rapamycin prevents epilepsy and early death, and late rapamycin suppresses established seizures.

Wong M.lab_name: Wong Lab, Department of Neurology, Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, Missouri, USA)
Wong M.role: Pediatric epileptologist whose lab studies how epilepsy develops, with a focus on mTOR in tuberous sclerosis complex and brain injury; senior author of the mouse study in which rapamycin prevented epilepsy in a TSC model.
Wong M.sub: Professor of Neurology, Pediatrics and Neuroscience, and Allen P. and Josephine B. Green Professor of Pediatric Neurology, Washington University in St. Louis · Director, Washington University Tuberous Sclerosis Center · pediatric neurology residency and epilepsy fellowship, Washington University · MD and PhD (neuroscience), UT Southwestern Medical School · BA, Princeton University
story: Michael Wong was senior author of the 2008 Annals of Neurology study led by Ling-Hui Zeng (ZEN2008). In mice lacking Tsc1 mainly in glia, rapamycin given before symptoms prevented epilepsy and early death, and rapamycin given after seizures had started suppressed them and prolonged survival, while reversing mTOR pathway activation and astrogliosis in the brain. The study, in mice, provided evidence that mTOR inhibition can act on epilepsy itself in TSC, and Wong was later a site investigator on the EXIST-3 trial of everolimus in patients (FRE2016).

Wong trained at Princeton and UT Southwestern, then in pediatric neurology and epilepsy at Washington University in St. Louis, where he has stayed. His lab studies epileptogenesis and seizure-induced brain injury in genetic and acquired rodent models, with the mTOR pathway as a central theme, and he directs the university's Tuberous Sclerosis Center.

highlights.ZEN2008: Senior author: rapamycin prevents epilepsy and early death in Tsc1 glial knockout mice, and suppresses seizures once they have begun.

French JA.lab_name: Comprehensive Epilepsy Center, NYU Grossman School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
French JA.role: Epilepsy clinical-trial specialist; first author of EXIST-3, the placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in which everolimus reduced treatment-resistant seizures in tuberous sclerosis complex.
French JA.sub: Professor of Neurology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine (since 2007) · Director, The Epilepsy Study Consortium · senior scientific roles at the Epilepsy Foundation · past president, American Epilepsy Society · earlier Professor of Neurology, University of Pennsylvania · epilepsy fellowships, Mount Sinai and Yale (1989) · MD, Brown University (1982)
story: Jacqueline French was first author of the EXIST-3 trial (FRE2016). 366 patients aged 2 to 65 with tuberous sclerosis complex and focal seizures that had not responded to standard drugs were randomised to placebo or to everolimus at a low or high blood level, added to their usual antiepileptic drugs. At least a 50% fall in seizure frequency was seen in 15.1% on placebo, 28.2% on low exposure and 40.0% on high exposure, with more adverse events at higher exposure. The trial showed a dose-dependent effect of mTOR inhibition on seizures in TSC over an 18-week core phase. It builds on mouse work such as ZEN2008.

French trained at Brown, Mount Sinai and Yale, was a professor of neurology at the University of Pennsylvania, and moved to NYU Langone in 2007. Her work centres on how antiseizure drugs are tested: she founded the Epilepsy Study Consortium, an academic network for early-phase epilepsy trials, and helped develop trial designs accepted by the FDA.

highlights.FRE2016: First author: in EXIST-3, adjunctive everolimus reduced treatment-resistant focal seizures in TSC in a dose-dependent way compared with placebo.

Hansen M.HAN2007: First author: lowering protein synthesis in C. elegans, by knocking down ribosomal proteins, the S6 kinase rsks-1 or translation-initiation factors, extended lifespan and raised heat-stress resistance, much as TOR inhibition does.

Kenyon C.HAN2007: Senior author: reducing translation extended lifespan in C. elegans, and the results linked TOR, but not sir-2.1, to the lifespan effect of dietary restriction.

Blagosklonny MV.ANI2011: Senior author: shows that intermittent rapamycin (2 weeks in every month) extends lifespan and delays spontaneous tumours in female 129/Sv inbred mice.

Richardson A.FIS2015: Co-author of the lifelong rapamycin health study in C57BL/6J mice, which found mixed and strongly sex-specific effects on healthspan measures rather than improvement across the board.
Richardson A.MAJ2012: Co-author of the study showing that rapamycin fed from 2 months of age, but not from 15 months, protected spatial memory in normally ageing mice, alongside lower brain IL-1beta.

Strong R.MAJ2012: Co-author: rapamycin started at 2 months of age, but not at 15 months, prevented age-related memory loss in mice, with lower IL-1beta and higher NMDA receptor signalling in the brain.

Oddo S.MAJ2012: Showed in normally ageing mice that rapamycin from 2 months of age preserved spatial memory at 18 months while a start at 15 months did not, with lower brain IL-1beta and higher NR2B and CREB phosphorylation; Oddo is senior author.

Lamming DW.YIL2012: Co-author: shows that calorie restriction boosts mouse intestinal stem cells by lowering mTORC1 in the neighbouring Paneth cells, an effect rapamycin copies.

Sengupta S.YIL2012: Co-author: calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 in Paneth cells, which then support more intestinal stem cells through the enzyme Bst1 (mice).

Sabatini DM.YIL2012: Senior author: calorie restriction expands mouse intestinal stem cells by lowering mTORC1 in the Paneth cells of their niche, not in the stem cells themselves, and rapamycin reproduces the effect.

Jones RG.PEA2009: Co-author: showed that CD8 T cells lacking TRAF6 fail to switch on fatty acid oxidation and form almost no memory cells, and that metformin or rapamycin increases memory CD8 T-cell formation in mice.

Delgoffe GM.POL2015: Co-author: mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer CD8 T cells differently, with constant mTORC1 driving short-lived glycolytic effectors and loss of mTORC2 favouring long-lived memory cells (mice).

Powell JD.POL2015: Senior author: shows that mTORC1 and mTORC2 separately shape CD8 T-cell fate in mice, with constant mTORC1 driving terminal effectors and loss of mTORC2 favouring memory cells.

Costa-Mattioli M.COS2009: Narrative review arguing that the start of mRNA translation, controlled by the mTORC1 and eIF2alpha pathways, is a main control point for long-lasting synaptic plasticity and long-term memory; Costa-Mattioli is first author.

Sonenberg N.COS2009: Senior author of a narrative review on how the mTORC1 and eIF2alpha pathways control the start of translation in long-lasting synaptic plasticity and long-term memory.
Sonenberg N.TAN2002: Co-author: mTOR, the 4E-BPs and eIF4E sit in hippocampal dendrites near synapses, and rapamycin reduced late-phase LTP and BDNF-induced potentiation in rodent hippocampal slices.
Sonenberg N.GKO2013: Senior author: mice lacking 4E-BP2 showed autism-like behaviours with increased translation of neuroligin mRNAs, and blocking eIF4E reversed the social deficit.

Gingras AC.TAN2002: Co-author: mTOR, 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2 and eIF4E sit in hippocampal dendrites near synapses, and rapamycin reduced late-phase LTP in rodent hippocampal slices.

Ruggero D.GKO2013: Co-author: shows that mice lacking 4E-BP2, the brake on eIF4E, have autism-like behaviours linked to increased translation of neuroligin mRNAs, reversed by a drug that blocks eIF4E.

Kozma SC.COT2006: Co-author with Daniela Cota (first author) and Randy Seeley (last author): hypothalamic mTOR signalling tracks energy status, and raising it with leucine in the brain lowers food intake and body weight (rats).

Thomas G.COT2006: Co-author: hypothalamic mTOR signalling acts as a fuel sensor in rats, with brain leucine lowering food intake and rapamycin blunting the effect of leptin on eating.

Ravikumar B.BER2006: Co-author: rapamycin-induced autophagy cleared several polyglutamine and polyalanine proteins in cells and reduced tau toxicity in flies.

Rubinsztein DC.BER2006: Senior author on the finding that rapamycin, by inducing autophagy, lowers the toxicity of several aggregate-prone proteins in cells and of tau in flies.

Sahin M.TSA2012: Senior author: deleting Tsc1 in cerebellar Purkinje cells caused autism-like behaviour in mice, and rapamycin started in early life prevented it.

Bateup HS.BAT2013: First author showing that Tsc1 loss in mouse hippocampal neurons weakens their inhibitory input and drives network hyperexcitability and seizure susceptibility, which rapamycin normalised.

Piccart M.PIC2014: First author of the final BOLERO-2 overall-survival report: everolimus plus exemestane kept its progression-free survival gain but did not significantly lengthen overall survival (31.0 vs 26.6 months).

Hortobagyi GN.PIC2014: Final overall-survival analysis of BOLERO-2: the progression-free survival gain held (7.8 vs 3.2 months) but overall survival was not significantly longer (31.0 vs 26.6 months, P = 0.14); Hortobagyi is a co-author (second author).

Baselga J.PIC2014: Senior author of the final BOLERO-2 overall-survival report, in which adding everolimus to exemestane did not significantly lengthen overall survival (31.0 vs 26.6 months), although the progression-free survival gain held.

Franz DN.FRA2006: First author: in five people with TSC, oral rapamycin shrank growing brain astrocytomas, and in one patient the tumour regrew when treatment was paused.
Franz DN.FRE2016: Senior author of EXIST-3, the phase 3 trial in which add-on everolimus reduced treatment-resistant seizures in TSC in a dose-dependent way (response 28% and 40% vs 15% on placebo).
